newsitem.title: USA: Low voter turnout expected on Penn. primary day.
newsitem.headline: Low voter turnout expected on Penn. primary day.

text.p: Low voter turnout was expected Tuesday as Pennsylvanians went to the polls to choose nominees for a range of municipal, judicial and school board races.

Mark Wolosik, Allegheny County's director of elections, predicted about 45 percent of Democratic voters and 35 percent of Republican voters would go to the polls, which were open from 7 A.M. to 8 P.M. EDT.

In Pittsburgh, the Democratic primary race for mayor will be the most closely watched contest, as Mayor Tom Murphy tries to defeat city Councilman Bob O'Connor and Chaston Roston, a neighbourhood activist. Harry Frost is the sole Republican candidate.

Murphy has been the leader by a wide margin in the polls in recent weeks. O'Connor, second to Murphy in the polls, has charged the mayor with mismanaging the city and paying too much attention to development projects.
Pittsburghers were also voting in a referendum on whether to create a civilian review board to monitor police discipline, the subject of heated debate between police officials and community leaders.
Discussions about the creation of a review board gained momentum after the October 1995 death of Jonny Gammage, a black motorist who died while in the custody of five white police officers.
Gammage's death and other cases in which police officers have been accused of excessive force sparked an outcry, which led to the referendum being placed on the ballot.

The judicial races include one opening on the state Supreme Court, four positions on Superior Court and one opening on Commonwealth Court. In Pittsburgh, the primary for the Court of Common Pleas, where two seats are open, will be closely watched.
Allegheny County District Attorney Bob Colville is one of 14 challengers. Colville has been district attorney for 22 years and formerly was Pittsburgh's chief of police.
